questionsToConsider: Is this about one product, a service or the company as a whole, and does the wording say so?
Which statements in the grid reflect claims you make in your marketing?
Do you want to compare new and long-standing customers, and is the tenure question enough for that?
Who will act on the negative answers, and how quickly?
guide.howToUseResponses: Read the written reasons alongside the feeling score, because the same score can come from very different experiences. In the statement grid, look for rows where agreement is weak; those are the promises customers don't believe yet. Compare new and long-standing customers, and if views get worse with time, look at what happens after the first few months rather than at your onboarding.
customizeSteps: Name your product in the greeting and the first questions so there's no doubt what people are rating.
Rewrite the grid statements to match the claims you make, such as saves time or good for beginners.
Send it to active customers and track the feeling score over time in the dashboard, or export results to CSV.

faqs.q: What is a customer attitudes survey?
faqs.a: It measures how customers feel about your product, service or brand and, importantly, why. It combines a rating with open questions so each score comes with context.

faqs.q: How is an attitude different from a preference?
faqs.a: An attitude is a broad opinion or feeling about something. A preference is a choice between options. This survey covers attitudes; a consumer preference survey covers choices.

faqs.q: Why use agree and disagree statements?
faqs.a: Statements let you test specific beliefs, such as whether customers think you're worth the price, in a way you can compare over time. Keep each statement to one idea so the answer is clear.

faqs.q: How often should I run a customer attitudes survey?
faqs.a: Every six months or so works for most products, and after any major change such as a redesign or price change. Keep the core questions the same to compare results.
